prompt: In a threat model, what is a trust boundary?

choices.text: The edge of the model's context window
choices.why: That is a limit on length; it says nothing about who runs what.

choices.text: The line between the read tools and the write tools
choices.why: That is lesson 10's question about access, asked of tools.

choices.text: Any firewall placed in front of the servers
choices.why: A firewall may sit on a boundary; the boundary itself is about who controls each side.

choices.text: Where zones run by different parties meet
choices.why: Right: data passing there leaves the hands of whoever looked after it.

prompt: With `--text`, how many of the twelve flows does `guard flows` mark for review?
hint: The last line of the capture.

prompt: Why does the zone rule alone leave `f6`, the attachment text, unmarked?
hint: Compare the zones of its two ends.

choices.text: The gate of lesson 10 has already read the attachment
choices.why: The gate reads proposed tool calls, never attachments.

choices.text: Both of its ends run on Tarefa's servers
choices.why: Right: the rule compares zones, and the client who wrote the text is not a zone.

choices.text: The flow carries a file's name and no text
choices.why: It carries the attachment's text, which is the problem.

choices.text: Clients cannot attach files in this application
choices.why: `f12` is exactly that upload.

prompt: Which flows does `--text` mark that the zone rule did not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Inside Tarefa's zone, written by somebody else.

choices.text: `f4`, the message on its way to the assistant
choices.why: Yes: a client wrote it.

choices.text: `f5`, the help centre pages
choices.why: Tarefa wrote them, so the text rule leaves them alone.

choices.text: `f6`, the attachment text
choices.why: Yes: a client wrote it.

choices.text: `f9`, the proposed tool call
choices.why: Yes: the model wrote it.

choices.text: `f10`, the tool's query to the orders database
choices.why: Tarefa's tool code builds it, from arguments the gate already checked.

choices.text: `f11`, what the log keeps
choices.why: Yes: it holds the client's words and the model's.

prompt: Tarefa adds a feature: the assistant reads a freelancer's profile, stored in Tarefa's database and written by the freelancer, to recommend people for a job. How does it enter the diagram?
hint: Who wrote the text, and where does it run?

choices.text: Not at all, because Tarefa's own database is trusted
choices.why: Where text is stored does not say who wrote it.

choices.text: As a move of the database into the internet zone
choices.why: The database still runs on Tarefa's servers; zones describe where code runs.

choices.text: As a flow to the assistant that `--text` marks
choices.why: Right: it stays in Tarefa's zone and carries a freelancer's words.

choices.text: As a second flow from the assistant to the provider
choices.why: `f7` already carries every prompt there; the new text arrives before it.

prompt: Match each STRIDE letter to the failure the lesson gives for it at Tarefa.
hint: One failure on the right belongs to no letter.

pairs.right: a client acting as another client's account
a reply nobody can tie to its prompt
one partner spending the month's budget
a tool call reaching another client's order

right_distractors: a reply that takes a second longer than usual

prompt: In an LLM application, which STRIDE letter takes in text that changes what the model does?
hint: Data that is no longer what it was.

choices.text: T, tampering
choices.why: Right: the lesson's one adjustment to STRIDE.

choices.text: I, information disclosure
choices.why: Disclosure is data reaching the wrong reader; this is the model being steered.

choices.text: E, elevation of privilege
choices.why: It may lead there, through a tool call; the letter for the text itself is another.

choices.text: S, spoofing
choices.why: Spoofing is about who somebody is, not about what the text does.

prompt: How many entries in Tarefa's register have a risk of 9?
Why do impact and likelihood run from 1 to 3 rather than as decimals?

choices.text: STRIDE defines exactly three levels of risk
choices.why: STRIDE names kinds of failure; it sets no scale.

choices.text: Python multiplies whole numbers faster than it multiplies decimals
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it; the register has twelve rows.

choices.text: Three levels keep the JSON file shorter
choices.why: The file is the same length either way.

choices.text: Nobody measured them, and a decimal would pretend they had
choices.why: Right: the scale is coarse because the judgement is.

prompt: When an entry's `control` is `null`, `guard threats` prints it as ___ in the control column.
Why does `threats.py` check the register against the diagram instead of only against itself?
hint: What can a list not report?

choices.text: A list cannot report a threat nobody wrote into it
choices.why: Right: the diagram says which flows should have been reviewed.

choices.text: The diagram holds better ratings than the register does
choices.why: The diagram holds no ratings at all.

choices.text: Sorting the entries by risk needs the diagram
choices.why: Sorting needs only impact and likelihood.

choices.text: Every flow must carry exactly one entry
choices.why: `f1` carries two, and that is normal.

prompt: `T2` is written against `f1`. On which other flow does it also belong, and why?
hint: Where does its first control read the message?

choices.text: `f7`, because the prompt crosses to the provider
choices.why: `T6` covers what crosses there; `check-in` runs before the prompt is built.

choices.text: `f4`, as `check-in` reads the message there
choices.why: Right: the threat lives where its control sits.

choices.text: `f2`, because the reply goes back to the client
choices.why: That is where `filter` works, on output; T2 is about the incoming message.

choices.text: `f11`, because the log keeps the message
choices.why: The log is another threat, `T9`, about retention.

prompt: Which habits does the lesson give for keeping a threat model true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It lives in the repository beside the code
choices.why: Yes: a pull request can change it.

choices.text: A feature adds its entries in the same pull request
choices.why: Yes: the new flow arrives with its review.

choices.text: The check runs in the build, where the tests run
choices.why: Yes: lesson 23 does that.

choices.text: It is rewritten from nothing every quarter
choices.why: Rewriting loses the reasons; keeping it current is the point.

choices.text: One person owns every rating, to keep them consistent
choices.why: The lesson asks for two people rating and comparing.

prompt: What exit status does `guard threats --open --text` return in the capture?
Put the steps of the threat model in the order the lesson takes them.
items: Draw the components and the zones they run in
Mark the flows that cross a zone or carry outside text
Ask the six STRIDE questions of each marked flow
Rate each threat's impact and likelihood
Name the control, or leave the threat open

prompt: Tarefa starts sending each reply to a second provider for translation and adds that flow to `flows.json`, with no new entry in the register. What does `guard threats` do?
hint: The new flow ends in another zone.

choices.text: It ranks the flow at the top with risk 9
choices.why: Nothing rates a flow that has no entry.

choices.text: It prints nothing new, since the register is unchanged
choices.why: It reads the diagram too, and the diagram changed.

choices.text: It reports the flow as UNREVIEWED and exits with 1
choices.why: Right: a crossing flow with no entry is exactly what it looks for.

choices.text: It refuses to run until the flow has an entry
choices.why: It runs and reports; the exit status is what fails a build.

prompt: Match each threat to the lesson that answers it.
hint: One lesson on the right answers none of the three.

pairs.left: T11, an upload carrying text that steers the model
T10, a reply not traceable to its prompt
T6, personal data reaching the provider

prompt: What does a threat register not do, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Tell whether a likelihood of 1 should have been 3
choices.why: Right: it records judgement and cannot check it.

choices.text: Rank the threats by impact times likelihood
choices.why: That is exactly what `guard threats` prints.

choices.text: Name the control that answers each threat
choices.why: The `control` column does that.

choices.text: List the threats that have no control yet
choices.why: `--open` lists them.
